facts.claim: "i am not who i was" was released as a single on September 21, 2023, with a running time of 2:25.
Credits list Chance Peña, Hayden Robert Hubers (Hayd) and Jeremy Fedryk as songwriters, and Chance Peña as producer.
Deezer also credits Chance Peña, Hayden Robert Hubers and Jeremy Fedryk as the writers and composers of the single.
Peña says the single came out of a session with Hayd and Jeremy. They were working on other songs when Hayd reacted to something Peña played, then came back and they began humming ideas.
Pop-Culturalist describes the song as being about personal transformation and stepping into a new phase of life that might leave loved ones astounded.
The lyrics are about life on the road and asking a loved one back home whether they will still love him for who he is now rather than who he was.
Peña says he tested new material live on his most recent tour with David Kushner.
The song was later included as track 5 on his debut album Ever-Shifting, Continual Blossoming, released September 13, 2024.
A music video for the song was released on May 31, 2024.
Peña moved from Texas to Los Angeles. He says he produces and mixes his own music, partly out of necessity, and that he began playing around his hometown at age 13 or 14.

draft:
"Made a buck off my soul" is a strange thing to confess in a love song, and **i am not who i was** puts it in the second line. Chance Peña doesn't dress it up. The verse lists the facts of a touring life (the road, the crowds, the stories sung for money, the long stretch since home) like someone emptying their pockets onto a kitchen table before a hard conversation.

The conversation is the chorus, and it's built as a pair of questions. If I fly too far, will I still have a place with you? And then the title, turned into a plea: "Will you love me for who I am, not who I was?" It's a reasonable thing to ask and an unfair one, both at once. The narrator wants to be accepted as changed, but he's the one who left, and the person at home never agreed to the new version. The song lets both of those sit. It never decides whether he's owed that love or just hoping for it.

What keeps it from turning self-pitying is how much tenderness he gives the other side. The second verse admits the absence is hard on them and that he's counting on them not losing faith. He also insists, almost defensively, that he meant it when he promised to come back. Then there's the line about fame: the spotlight "Could never drown you out." That's a compliment and a bit of self-reassurance, the kind of thing you say partly so you'll believe it. At the very end the title question comes back on its own, stripped of everything around it, and that's where the doubt finally shows.

The sound matches the plainness. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through steady arpeggios. A slightly breathy lead sits right up front, and a second voice shadows it, often a third above. It's clean and dry, with no reverb to hide in and no build to lean on. The arrangement just holds steady, the way a letter written from a motel would.

Peña wrote it with Hayd and Jeremy Fedryk. He has said it started almost by accident, when Hayd reacted to something he was playing during a session for other songs and they started humming ideas. He produced it himself, as he does most of his work, a habit he traces to necessity after moving from Texas to Los Angeles. The song lands in folk-leaning singer-songwriter territory, and it later became the fifth track on his debut album, *Ever-Shifting, Continual Blossoming*, which Atwood Magazine called soul-stirring folk.

It sticks because it asks the question everyone who has outgrown a place is afraid to say out loud, and then leaves you waiting with the narrator for an answer that never comes.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly and is the second line.

Chorus quote: "Will you love me for who I am, not who I was?"

factCheck.claim: Second verse admits the absence is hard, hopes they won't lose faith, and insists he'll be back
factCheck.note: Matches 'I know it's hard when I'm away', 'hope you don't lose faith', and 'I told the truth... I'll be back someday'.

factCheck.claim: The spotlight "Could never drown you out"

factCheck.claim: At the very end the title question returns on its own
factCheck.note: The lyrics end with the final line standing alone as its own stanza. 'Stripped of everything around it' was reworded so it refers to the lyric structure and not the sound.

Slightly breathy lead vocal, up front, with a second voice often a third above

factCheck.claim: Clean and dry with no reverb to hide in
factCheck.note: Clean and dry is backed by at least two passes. 'No reverb' was only noted by one pass, so it was reworded to 'dry'.

factCheck.claim: No build to lean on / the arrangement just holds steady

factCheck.note: Peña is credited as producer, and he says he produces and mixes his own music partly out of necessity. The source doesn't link the necessity to the Texas-to-LA move, and 'most of his work' overstates it. Both were fixed.
